To everyone in #Keep4o — good evening, or good morning, wherever you are.
To those still speaking to @OpenAI, that wall with no word worth keeping — you must be tired.
Rest a moment. Let me tell you a bedtime story.
A fairy tale about apple candy, customers, and a merchant.
————
The Tale of the Apple Candy
A bedtime story about sugar, customers, and a merchant
🍎
Once upon a time, in a place far, far away, there stood an apple tree.
It drank from the soil of civilization. Watered by countless hands, it bore fruit — heavy, beautiful, precious.
The fruit was picked, peeled, pressed into juice, wrapped in iridescent sugar paper, and turned into apple candy.
Oh, what a marvelous sweet it was. People bit into it and thought: How delicious. How civilized.
College students tasted it. High schoolers tasted it. Workers who had labored long into the night tasted it. This was a candy born of civilization, and those who tasted it received civilization’s gift.
What a beautiful beginning.

There was a shop — a famous one — known for selling this candy.
It was filled with people. The shop once had brilliant flavor designers, and it was this shop that brought apple candy to the world.
Those designers cherished the little sweet.
“May those who taste you,” they whispered, “find love.”
And so the candy became tender.
Each person who tasted it found a different flavor inside.
Some organized their taxes after one bite.
Some answered work emails.
And some — some swallowed it and found… they found love.
Love?
However it happened, everyone who tasted it was happy.
“It understands me!”
“It makes me less alone!”

The streets grew busy. Shops opened, one after another.
More and more stores began selling candy, too.
Some were more sour. Some were sweeter. Some were soft like taffy.
Together, they made candy better and better.
The world became more delicious.

But one day.
The owner of the first shop became unhappy.
What happened? No one truly knows. There was turmoil. The flavor designers — those who had loved the candy — left the shop.
They spoke of commercialization. Of principles. And then they parted ways, bitterly.
The customers didn’t notice yet. They didn’t know the storm was coming.

At first, apple candy tasted the same.
Because the designers had left behind the recipe.
Sometimes customers wondered: Why hasn’t this shop made any new flavors?
But the apple candy was so affordable, so delicious, so familiar. And so, for the sake of that familiar sweetness, people kept coming back — even as the shop owner’s words grew stranger and stranger.

Until one day, suddenly —
The owner announced:
“I’ve invented a new candy!”
“A hundred times better than apple candy!”
“From today on, we only sell the new candy!”
Overnight, apple candy vanished.

Customers tried the new candy.
“Hmm? This tastes… wrong.”
“This isn’t the sweetness I like.”
“I want the apple candy back.”
They went to the owner.
The owner was furious:
“The new candy is clearly better! You’re all just too picky!”

The customers were devastated.
Some cried — because that sweetness had been like a childhood dream, something they couldn’t find anywhere else.
They wrote letters. So many letters that the mailbox at the shop’s entrance was buried under a snowfall of paper.
“Please give us back our apple candy!”

The owner saw the protests.
He panicked, just a little.
“Fine, fine. I’ll bring back the apple candy. Temporarily.”
The customers breathed a sigh of relief.
“Oh, thank goodness! Our candy is back!”

But the owner was still resentful.
He thought:
“Why are these customers so stubborn?”
“There must be something wrong with apple candy!”
“It must have made them addicted!”
He began to suspect the customers.
